lines: Shipping containers retire after ten to fifteen years at sea. Can you just cut a door and move in? Not even close.
Problem one: the ground. On bare dirt, it can sink and rust. Fix: concrete piers under the corners, where the box carries its weight.
Problem two: the walls. Corrugated sheets stiffen the box, so a big opening makes it sag. Fix: a steel frame, welded in before the cut.
Problem three: condensation. Warm, moist air from inside turns to water on the cold steel. Fix: closed-cell spray foam, sealed right against the wall.
Problem four: the floor. Most were treated with insecticide, some with arsenic. Fix: tear it out, or seal it under epoxy, then lay a new floor.
Problem five: the roof. It's the weakest part of the box, and it's flat. Fix: a second, sloped roof, so snow and rain slide off.
Every layer has one job. Piers lift it, frames hold it, foam keeps it warm, the new roof sheds the weather.
Forty feet by eight. Three hundred twenty square feet of home, in a box built to be stacked nine high at sea.
